rules: use the cases as seeds; original wording and numbers
no memorisation; a tip with every term used
every abbreviation spelled out at first use

cases.name: Ordering of spent outputs
cases.idea: A chain of successively spent transaction outputs. Ask the order of the transactions. A spending transaction always comes after the transaction whose output it spends, traceable back to the coinbase transaction.

cases.name: Mined or not
cases.idea: A set of transactions with spending references. A transaction that receives a spending reference means the referenced transaction was already mined. Ask which are mined and which are not (same question as C1 or separate).

cases.name: Full spending
cases.idea: If no change output is added, the unspent difference is the fee and the miner collects it. Ask the change amount (or the fee) for a transaction with several inputs and several outputs, with simple numbers.

topics.topic: approval without private keys (what a signature proves)
telling a genuine from a fake transaction
why seed words replaced hand-managed random keys

points.point: Total inputs versus total outputs, with and without a fee.
Block reward by height with the halving interval; legal versus illegal coinbase; toy numbers; halving ends at the 1 satoshi level; the names satoshi and bitcoin are given, not recorded on chain.
All coins are minted by miners; inputs trace back to a coinbase.
Each block links to the previous block, so miners restart on a new block.
Hash trials are unpredictable; the requirement is a value below a difficulty target, adjusted after a fixed number of blocks.
The 10-minute rule and soft forks: how the steady block interval and the difficulty adjustment protect against forking risk.

coverage_required: Every one of T1-T9, A-F and G-P is reported as the item key that covers it, partial, or the word GAP.

points2.point: Coinbase amount calculation with and without fees; matching reward to block number; after minting ends the coinbase is fees only; the first blocks' (Satoshi's) coinbase amounts; total mined over a full halving era or selected blocks; varied numbers per case.
The first spend and the first valuation transaction (the pizza) explained in class: today's value of that pizza, easy arithmetic only.

Hash capacity of Bitcoin, the 10-minute rule and the bitcoin price depend on each other; hash rate rises over time and changes hardware requirements; the risk in the exact time a single miner finds a block; mining pools and how they reduce that risk.
Miners collect transactions but block size is limited, so they choose by fee per size, not by amount transferred, unlike traditional systems.
Why digital money did not work before Bitcoin: double spending, balance modification, risks of central authorities, the cost of preventing these in traditional digital money; how Bitcoin solves each.
Why old currencies are no longer used (Ottoman money; TL to YTL and back to TL): what if ancestors left millions in an old currency, and why this does not happen with Bitcoin.
People losing access to private keys; current best-practice techniques.
Why a transaction input cannot carry its own confirmation script; how Bitcoin solves it (input and output locking and unlocking scripts must run together and succeed).
Who confirms transactions, how they are distributed, why only genuine transactions have a chance, what happens if a fake source publishes fake transactions or blocks and how the system reacts.
The 51 percent rule, how a 51 percent attack can happen, and the protection mechanisms.
